Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity: A Taiwanese case and review 
of literature

ARTICLE INFO  
Keywords: 
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and 
myoclonus (PERM), glycine receptor 
Immunotherapy 
ABSTRACT  
Introduction: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) is a rare disorder. However, the 
outcome is still variable with different serological and tumor associations, and the elements to good response 
with less relapse is yet to be elucidated. 
Method: We present a case and obtain a literature review of patients with PERM and make comparisons based on 
different serological groups. We also analyze patients with idiopathic PERM that had detailed medical records. 
Results: 81 patients were collected and analyzed. The largest group were glycine receptor-antibody (GlyR-Ab)- 
positive (70%), and the seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative group had better response to immunotherapy. Malignancy 
can occur up to 2 years from the presentation of PERM. Among the 18 cases with detailed records, the patients 
who had good outcome initiate immunotherapy within 2 months from presentation. 9 of the 12 patients who 
experienced no relapse had non-steroid immunotherapy. The maximal interval time of relapse was 24 months. 
Conclusion: We recommend tumor surveillance up to 2 years in patients with PERM and early administration of 
immunotherapies and maintain with non-steroid immunotherapy with or without oral corticosteroid for a 
minimum of 2 years to reduce the risk of relapse in GlyR-Ab-positive patients.   
1. Introduction 
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) 
is a rare disorder that is considered part of the stiff-person syndrome 
spectrum disorder (SPSD). Besides the shared presentation of limb and 
truncal rigidity, stimulus-sensitive muscle spasms, myoclonus, and 
hyperekplexia, PERM has additional brainstem symptoms, including 
oculomotor palsies, nystagmus and ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria, and 
trismus [1] . Antibodies to the glycine receptor (GlyR) occur in approx -
imately 50% of cases of PERM [2] , which are found either in isolation or 
less frequently in combination with glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) 
antibodies [3] , anti-dipeptidyl peptidase-like protein 6 (DPPX) anti -
bodies [4] , and amphiphysin antibodies [5] . It is unclear how the 
serological results represents as to treatment response and relapse; we 
obtain a literature review of all previously reported cases with PERM 
and make comparisons based on different serological groups. 
Though there is heterogeneity in clinical manifestation, the glycine 
receptor-antibody (GlyR-Ab)-positive cases often show remarkable and 
sustained response to immunotherapy [1] . Nevertheless, there are still 
variations in responsiveness to immunotherapy. Also, most of the review

articles focus mainly on management of SPSD as a whole [6] . Here, we 
present a patient in Taiwan with PERM associated with GlyR-Ab with a 
complete resolution of symptoms and no relapse within 3 years of 
follow-up. By demonstrating our case and all the previously reported 
patients with PERM without tumor association as a confounding factor 
and with detailed medical history and management records, we hope to 
find key elements in disease control of this rare disease. 
2. Methods 
We present a case with PERM. The literature review aimed to identify 
all the reported cases of PERM until the end of 2020. We searched 
through PubMed database using the following words: ‘progressive 
encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus, ’ “ autoimmune 
encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus, ’ and ‘PERM. ’ We 
searched lists of identi fi ed reference papers to fi nd additional papers not

captured by the initial search strategy. All identified articles were read 
in full with relevant data extracted. 
Another aim is to find the elements in getting a good response to 
immunotherapy in the patients with PERM without the confounding 
factor of tumor association. We obtain details records of the following of 
all the reported patients with idiopathic PERM: the time from symptoms 
onset to immunotherapy initiation, the types of immunotherapies, the 
disease severities in terms of Modified Rankin Scale (mRS) before and 
after immunotherapies, and the occurrence of relapse under the type of 
immunotherapy for maintenance. 
3. Results 
3.1. Case presentation 
A 46-year-old man presented in June 2017 with 2 weeks of right 
facial numbness and episodic facial muscle spasms after a preceding 
upper respiratory tract infection. The episodic spasms progressed to 
involve the masticatory muscles resulting in trismus. A week later, the 
facial numbness had spread to the left side with additional vertical 
binocular diplopia and left arm stimulus-sensitive myoclonus. Neuro -
logic examination was otherwise normal. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) 
contained 4 lymphocytes/mL, and other data were normal. Brain mag -
netic resonance imaging (MRI) scan was normal. Blink reflexes showed 
excessive facial muscle activities on the right when elicited by sub -
maximal electrical stimulation on either side of the supraorbital branch 
of trigeminal nerve and a synkinesis of orbicularis oculi and oris. 
Therapeutic trial with empirical antibiotic (ampicillin, doxycycline) and 
antiviral agents (acyclovir) did not show any response. Anti-Yo, -Hu, -Ri, 
-amphiphsyin, -CV2, -Ma2/Ta, -Recoverin, -SOX1, -Titin, -Zic4, -GAD65, 
and – Tr (DNER) antibodies were negative, and extensive investigation 
with whole-body positron emission tomography – computed tomography 
(PET-CT) scan ruled out an occult neoplasm. Due to the worsening of 
diplopia and facial contractions despite 3 days of hydrocortisone 100 mg 
twice daily, he received 5 days of 1 g/d of intravenous methylprednis -
olone (IvMP) until vertical diplopia and left arm myoclonus disappeared 
after 5 days. He was discharged under the diagnosis of post-infectious 
brainstem encephalitis and did not receive further immunotherapy. 
However, 2 weeks later, he developed much more severe symptoms 
with complete horizontal ophthalmoplegia and persistent contractions 
of the bilateral masseter muscles. Though his consciousness remained 
clear with no limb involved, he developed agitation and laryngeal spasm 
resulting difficulty in swallowing and further apnea, for which he was 
intubated. Repeated brain MRI scan and CSF were still negative. Because 
the symptoms seemed to suggest dysfunction and/or hyperexcitability 
confined to the brainstem, a diagnosis of PERM was made. We gave 5 
days of 1 g/d IvMP followed by 5 sessions of plasmapheresis (PP), which 
were immediately boosted with 500 mg/d IvMP in the last 3 sessions. 
After we gave 0.4 g/kg intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) for 5 days, 
the symptoms slowly disappeared, and he was extubated 3 weeks later 
and discharged. Fig. 1 showed the clinical and treatment course details 
and evaluated clinical measures using mRS score. Upon discharge, he 
received azathioprine 60 mg/d and oral prednisolone 60 mg every other 
day. At follow-up 6 months later, he was free of myoclonus and spasm

with a sequela of only slight limitation of gaze to the left, which also 
disappeared slowly over 6 months. His oral azathioprine was maintained 
for 2 years while prednisolone tapered by 10 mg every 2 months until 
reaching 20 mg and 5 mg every 3 months until cessation. He remained 
symptom free without relapse to current report dated after 3 years from 
symptom onset. 
The patient ’ s sera and CSF, which were collected right before 
receiving plasmapheresis, tested positive for GlyR-Ab in the Autoim -
mune Neurology Diagnostic Laboratory, University of Oxford ( Supple -
mentary Data 1 ) 3 months after the symptom onset. 
3.2. Literature review 
We identi fi ed 80 cases of PERM in 45 articles, and, with the current 
case reported, there was an overall of 81 cases with PERM ( Supple -
mentary Data 2 ) [1,4,5,7 – 48] . The results are summarized in Table 1 
and was categorized based on the following serology results: 
GlyR-Ab-positive, seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative, and seronegative. The 
largest group were GlyR-Ab-positive (n = 57, 70% of the total), the 
second group were GlyR-Ab-negative but positive in other antibodies 
(GAD, n = 9; DPPX, n = 3; anti-amphiphysin, n = 1) (n = 13, 16% of 
the total), and the remaining were either untested or no autoimmunity 
were identified (n = 11, 14% of the total). Male were slightly more 
predominant in the GlyR-Ab-positive (68%) and seronegative groups 
(64%) while being less in the seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative group 
(46%). The age of onset ranged from 1 to 81 years with a widespread in 
all groups. The mean age of onset was younger in the seronegative group 
with 41.27 years compared to 49.28 years in the GlyR-Ab-positive group 
and 52.38 years in the seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative group. 
Pre-existing other autoimmune conditions were more prevalent in 
the seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative group (2/13, 15%) than the GlyR-Ab- 
positive group (2/31, 6%). Only a few cases in the GlyR-Ab-positive and 
seronegative groups showed abnormal MRI results. Tumor association in 
patients with PERM overall is modest (18/81, 22%), which was slightly 
more prevalent in the seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative group (31% versus 
24% in GlyR-Ab-positive group and 9% in the seronegative group). 2 
cases in the GlyR-Ab-positive group had pre-existed malignancies before 
the symptoms of PERM, one being breast cancer and thymoma had co-

existed GAD antibody and another being Hodgkin ’ s lymphoma. 1 case in 
the seronegative group had Hodgkin ’ s lymphoma before the symptoms 
of PERM. Tumors were found during or after the presentation of PERM 
in 10 of the 51 GlyR-Ab-positive patients, including thymoma (n = 4), 
Hodgkin ’ s lymphoma (n = 3), lung cancer (n = 2), and breast cancer 
(n = 1), 4 of the 14 seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative group, including 
thymoma (n = 2), breast cancer (n = 1), and lung cancer (n = 1), and 2 
of the 10 seronegative group, including renal cell carcinoma (n = 1) and 
Hodgkin ’ s lymphoma (n = 1). Note that 2 cases with breast cancer were 
found remotely from the presentation of PERM, which 1 relating to 
GlyR-Ab was found 18 months later, and 1 relating to anti-amphiphysin 
antibody was found 2 years later. 
The seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative group showed a better response 
to immunotherapy than GlyR-Ab-positive group (54% versus 46% with 
substantial response of mRS 0 or 1 after immunotherapy, respectively; 
38% versus 33% with partial response of mRS 2 or 3 after immuno -
therapy, respectively). The seronegative group responded poor with 
only 18% responded substantially and 9% responded partially. Of the 
seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative group, the patients with anti-DPPX an -
tibodies showed better response to immunotherapy with 67% (2/3) 
compared to 44% (4/9) in patients with anti-GAD antibodies with 
substantial response. Only 1 patient had an anti-amphiphysin antibody 
and had substantial response to immunotherapy. 
The relapse rate seems to be higher in the seropositive-GlyR-Ab- 
negative group (40%, 4/10) as compared to 23% in the GlyR-Ab- 
positive group (10/43), though it was not statistically significant 
(p = 0.241 using Chi-square test). However, none of the patients in the 
seronegative group showed relapse. And due to a lack of detailed 
medical records or follow-up, only 3 patients were acquired in this 
calculation. Of the 6 GlyR-Ab-positive patients that had a clear 
description of the time of relapse after immunotherapy without the 
confounding factor of tumor management, the median time of relapse 
was 14 months, 16.5 months in the 2 patients of the seropositive-GlyR- 
Ab-negative group (datas not shown). 
3.3. Management record 
Detailed documentation of management was obtained in a total of 18 
patients from 15 articles (see Table 2 ), including our current case. 9 
patients reached good outcomes after immunotherapy (mRS 1 or 0). Of 
these 9 patients, all had steroid-based immunotherapy and 6 initiate 
some kind of immunotherapy within 2 months. 7 of these 9 patients had 
IvMP, and 7 patients required another kind of immunotherapy [i.e., PP 
or plasma exchange (PEx), IVIg] despite steroid-based immunotherapy if 
initiate immunotherapy after 1 month from symptom onset. 
Of the 6 patients who had relapse, 3 patients had relapse while under 
no immunotherapy for maintenance.The other 3 patients had relapse 
while under oral corticosteroid either with maintenance or dose 
reduction. 12 patients experienced no relapse, and 9 of these patients 
had non-steroid immunotherapy with or without oral corticosteroid.

4. Discussion 
We report a case with idiopathic GlyR-Ab-positive PERM, who, after 
within 1 month of disease recognition and thereafter applied aggressive 
immunotherapies, had a complete resolution of symptoms after 1 year 
during 1 year off treatment, and no relapse within 3 years of follow-up. 
Our most updated literature review of 81 patients with PERM showed 
that the largest group were GlyR-Ab-positive (70%). The seropositive- 
GlyR-Ab-negative group had a better response to immunotherapy than 
the GlyR-Ab-positive group but with a seemingly higher relapse rate but 
no statistically significance. Moreover, though the association with 
malignancy is modest, but malignancy, especially breast cancer, can 
occur remotely from the presentation of PERM. Therefore, regular tumor 
surveillance for up to 2 years is recommended. By demonstrating our 
case along with all the previously reported patients with PERM without 
tumor association as a confounding factor and with detailed medical 
history and management records, we stress the importance of early 
recognition of this disorder with early administration of intensive 
steroid-based immunotherapies and maintenance therapy with non- 
steroid immunotherapy with or without oral corticosteroid for a mini -
mum of 2 years to reduce the risk of relapse in GlyR-Ab-positive patients. 
There had been 3 literature reviews of PERM reported previously 
[41,45,49] , but only the one by Su et al. was made after the first case 
relating to GlyR-Ab was identified and reported in 2008. Su et al. [41] 
reviewed the clinical manifestations, serological results, tumor, MRI 
findings, management, and clinical outcomes of reported cases with 
PERM until 2020. Our study provides the most updated and compre -
hensive literature review to date as Su et al. had missed some of the 
cases. Furthermore, we focused on comparing different serological re -
sults with tumor association, treatment response, and, therefore, prog -
nosis and relapse. 
It is thought that 50% of the cases with PERM were related to GlyR- 
Ab [2] , and as more antibody testing are becoming more widely avail -
able, more GlyR-Ab-positive cases have been reported (70%, 57/81 
cases in our literature review). Indeed, PERM remains to be the most 
common symptom in patients with GlyR-Ab (63%) [1] , which may vary 
slightly depending on the case series collected (47.6% in Swayne) [21] . 
Other antibodies reported relating to PERM have been anti-GAD, 
anti-DPPX, and anti-amphiphysin (16%), and 13% were seronegative. 
The association with tumor is modest in the patients with PERM (18/ 
81, 22%). As most of the tumors were found during the presentation of 
PERM (13/15), 2 cases with breast cancer were found remotely from the 
presentation of PERM, which 1 relating to GlyR-Ab was found 18 months 
later and 1 relating to anti-amphiphysin antibody was found 2 years 
later. The association of anti-amphiphysin antibody with other SPSD 
symptoms and breast cancer was known [50] . We recommend that 
whole body CT in evaluating tumor is necessary at the time of presen -
tation with PERM and follow-ups with a minimum of 2 years, especially 
with breast cancer. 
The results in patients with GlyR-Ab-positive were coincided with 
the previous literature review by Swayne et al. on the response to 
immunotherapy that 46% of the patients with GlyR-Ab-positive PERM/

SPSD responded substantially to immunotherapy and 33% responded 
partially [21] . In our literature review of all the reported patients with 
PERM, the seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative group had better response to 
immunotherapy than GlyR-Ab-positive group. Among the 
seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative group, the patients with anti-DPPX an -
tibodies showed better response to immunotherapy, with 67% (2/3) 
responded substantially.In contrast, only 44% (4/9) of patients with 
anti-GAD antibodies had substantial response to immunotherapy. These 
results are coincided with previous conclusion that it is the type of au -
toantibodies, not the type of syndrome, that predicts the outcome. Each 
antibody has different management and treatment responses as they 
stand for their own unique underlying pathophysiological mechanisms 
that reflect on links with autoimmune or paraneoplastic disease [3] . 
Neuronal surface antibodies (e.g., GlyR and DPPX) usually have better 
response to immunotherapy than those associated with intracellular 
antigen (e.g., GAD65) [3] . Though the seropositive-GlyR-Ab-negative 
group had a better response to immunotherapy than the 
GlyR-Ab-positive group; they also tends to have a higher relapse rate, 
though statistically insignificant. The median time of relapse was similar 
in both groups. 
Though nearly half of the patients with GlyR-Ab-positive responded 
remarkably to immunotherapy, we would still like to know the elements 
in achieving a good response, hoping to escalate the responsiveness and 
reduce relapse rate. Among the 18 cases from the literature review of all 
published cases/case series of idiopathic PERM with detailed clinical 
course and management with our current case, 7 out of 10 patients who 
had substantial response to immunotherapy initiate some kind of 
immunotherapy within 2 months. Moreover, though all had steroid- 
based immunotherapy, all except 1 of these patients required another 
kind of immunotherapy (i.e., PP or PEx, IVIg) if initiate immunotherapy 
after 1 month from symptom onset. Thus, we recommend early recog -
nition of clinical symptoms with early administration of intensive 
steroid-based immunotherapies and closely followed by other kind of 
immunotherapy, if initiated later or suboptimal response to initial 
immunotherapy. Also, there are still 23% of the patients with GlyR-Ab 
had relapse. All of the 6 patients who had relapse had either no immu -
notherapy for maintenance or were under oral corticosteroid with dose 
reduction. And 10 out of the 13 patients who had no relapse had non- 
steroid immunotherapy with or without oral corticosteroid. Because 
the maximal interval time of relapse was 24 months, we recommend 
non-steroid immunotherapy with or without oral corticosteroid for at 
least 2 years to reduce the risk of future relapse. 
5. Conclusion 
PERM is a rare disorder that often show a remarkable response to 
immunotherapy in patients with seropositivity, especially with GlyR-Ab 
and anti-DPPX antibodies. Nevertheless, there are still variations in 
responsiveness to immunotherapy. We obtained the most updated 
literature review of all patients with PERM. Tumor surveillance up to 2 
years is recommended. By demonstrating our case along with patients 
with PERM without tumor association as a confounding factor and with 
detailed medical history and management records, we recommend early 
recognition of this disorder with early administration of intensive

steroid-based immunotherapies and maintenance therapy with non- 
steroid immunotherapy for a minimum of 2 years to reduce the risk of 
relapse in patients with GlyR-Ab.

segments.text:
3.1. Case presentation 
A 46-year-old man presented in June 2017 with 2 weeks of right 
facial numbness and episodic facial muscle spasms after a preceding 
upper respiratory tract infection. The episodic spasms progressed to 
involve the masticatory muscles resulting in trismus. A week later, the 
facial numbness had spread to the left side with additional vertical 
binocular diplopia and left arm stimulus-sensitive myoclonus. Neuro -
logic examination was otherwise normal. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) 
contained 4 lymphocytes/mL, and other data were normal. Brain mag -
netic resonance imaging (MRI) scan was normal. Blink reflexes showed 
excessive facial muscle activities on the right when elicited by sub -
maximal electrical stimulation on either side of the supraorbital branch 
of trigeminal nerve and a synkinesis of orbicularis oculi and oris. 
Therapeutic trial with empirical antibiotic (ampicillin, doxycycline) and 
antiviral agents (acyclovir) did not show any response. Anti-Yo, -Hu, -Ri, 
-amphiphsyin, -CV2, -Ma2/Ta, -Recoverin, -SOX1, -Titin, -Zic4, -GAD65, 
and – Tr (DNER) antibodies were negative, and extensive investigation 
with whole-body positron emission tomography – computed tomography 
(PET-CT) scan ruled out an occult neoplasm. Due to the worsening of 
diplopia and facial contractions despite 3 days of hydrocortisone 100 mg 
twice daily, he received 5 days of 1 g/d of intravenous methylprednis -
olone (IvMP) until vertical diplopia and left arm myoclonus disappeared 
after 5 days. He was discharged under the diagnosis of post-infectious 
brainstem encephalitis and did not receive further immunotherapy. 
However, 2 weeks later, he developed much more severe symptoms 
with complete horizontal ophthalmoplegia and persistent contractions 
of the bilateral masseter muscles. Though his consciousness remained 
clear with no limb involved, he developed agitation and laryngeal spasm 
resulting difficulty in swallowing and further apnea, for which he was 
intubated. Repeated brain MRI scan and CSF were still negative. Because 
the symptoms seemed to suggest dysfunction and/or hyperexcitability 
confined to the brainstem, a diagnosis of PERM was made. We gave 5 
days of 1 g/d IvMP followed by 5 sessions of plasmapheresis (PP), which 
were immediately boosted with 500 mg/d IvMP in the last 3 sessions. 
After we gave 0.4 g/kg intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) for 5 days, 
the symptoms slowly disappeared, and he was extubated 3 weeks later 
and discharged. Fig. 1 showed the clinical and treatment course details 
and evaluated clinical measures using mRS score. Upon discharge, he 
received azathioprine 60 mg/d and oral prednisolone 60 mg every other 
day. At follow-up 6 months later, he was free of myoclonus and spasm

segments.text:
with a sequela of only slight limitation of gaze to the left, which also 
disappeared slowly over 6 months. His oral azathioprine was maintained 
for 2 years while prednisolone tapered by 10 mg every 2 months until 
reaching 20 mg and 5 mg every 3 months until cessation. He remained 
symptom free without relapse to current report dated after 3 years from 
symptom onset. 
The patient ’ s sera and CSF, which were collected right before 
receiving plasmapheresis, tested positive for GlyR-Ab in the Autoim -
mune Neurology Diagnostic Laboratory, University of Oxford ( Supple -
mentary Data 1 ) 3 months after the symptom onset.

segments.text:
We report a case with idiopathic GlyR-Ab-positive PERM, who, after 
within 1 month of disease recognition and thereafter applied aggressive 
immunotherapies, had a complete resolution of symptoms after 1 year 
during 1 year off treatment, and no relapse within 3 years of follow-up.
